missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to describe the similarities and distinctions between the planets, their moons, and artificial satellites.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson covers this only briefly in keyPoints[2].content: "Planets orbit the Sun. Moons are natural satellites that orbit planets. Artificial satellites are machines that people launch into orbit round the Earth. Gravity keeps all three in their orbits." It gives one similarity (gravity keeps them in orbit) and a few distinctions (what each orbits, natural versus artificial). It does not set them out as a comparison of similarities and distinctions. None of it appears in writeBullets, revisionCardBullets or the checkpoints.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: for circular orbits, the force of gravity can lead to changing velocity but unchanged speed
missing_spec_content.why: The spec asks students to "explain qualitatively". keyPoints[2].content only states the outcome: "the force of gravity can change the velocity without changing the speed. The speed stays the same, but the direction keeps changing." It does not explain why. In particular, it never says that velocity is a vector, so a change of direction alone is a change of velocity, or that gravity acts towards the centre, at right angles to the motion. This HT point is also missing from writeBullets, revisionCardBullets and the checkpoints.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: for a stable orbit, the radius must change if the speed changes.
missing_spec_content.why: The "Higher only" paragraph in keyPoints[2].content repeats this as a bare statement: "For a stable orbit, the radius must change if the speed changes." The earlier sentence "Higher orbits: the gravitational field is weaker... So a lower speed is needed" gives some reasoning, but it is not marked as HT. It is also not tied to the spec statement in the direction the spec asks for (speed change leading to radius change). No checkpoint tests it.

above_gcse.text: The resultant force directed towards the centre of a circle, keeping an object in circular motion — for orbits, this force is provided by gravity
above_gcse.why: The spec section does not use the term "centripetal force". It says only "Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites... to maintain their circular orbits." The lesson makes centripetal force a key term and repeats it throughout. This goes beyond the supplied spec wording and could confuse the student.

above_gcse.text: Say 'gravity provides the centripetal force needed for circular motion'.
above_gcse.why: This tells students to use the term "centripetal force" as if the mark scheme requires it. The supplied spec wording is "Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites... to maintain their circular orbits".

above_gcse.text: But it also has a high tangential velocity (sideways speed).
above_gcse.why: "Tangential velocity" does not appear in the spec section and is not needed. The lesson already glosses it as "sideways speed".

factual_errors.text: Artificial satellites are machines that people launch into orbit round the Earth.
factual_errors.correction: Artificial satellites can orbit other bodies as well as the Earth, for example probes orbiting the Moon or Mars. Many orbit the Earth, but the definition should not be limited to the Earth.

wrong_terms.text: Gravity provides the centripetal force that keeps the object in its curved path.
wrong_terms.spec_term: Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites (both natural and artificial) to maintain their circular orbits.

not_checked: Most of keyPoints[0] (mass vs weight, W = mg, gravitational field strength), keyPoints[1] (gravitational fields), the table of g values, checkpoints 0 and 1, and the examTip on g = 9.8 N/kg relate to specification content that was not supplied (e.g. weight and gravitational field strength sections). Their scientific accuracy was checked: W = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N; 70 × 9.8 = 686 N; 70 × 1.6 = 112 N; 70 × 3.7 = 259 N; Earth g / Moon g ≈ 6. Their wording and terms could not be compared with the specification text.
examTips[3]: "Examiners use it in every set of papers." This claim about exam papers cannot be verified from the specification text.
No diagrams are included (all "diagram" fields are null), so there was nothing visual to check.
